To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the legal enforcement of CNC can be efficient and that the law should be wary in policing CNCs to prevent contracting parties from agreeing to excessively broad CNC scope.

(1) a CNC is a hybrid that combines the remedies of specific performance (for movements within the CNC scope) and liquidated damages (for movements outside the CNC scope); (2) the appropriate CNC scope is determined by the optimal balance between the overinvestment tendency and the underinvestment effect; and (3) contracting parties have the incentive to overinvest in the CNC scope.

(a) the appropriate choice of the scope of CNCs can achieve first-best investment in human capital, and that (b) the law should be wary in policing CNCs because contracting parties have the incentive to overuse them.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the efficiency of CNCs in the presence of contract renegotiation.
how the law should police covenants not to work for competitors.
a fundamental question of contract theory: what are the optimal terms of a contract that balances the ex post and ex ante efficiency considerations?
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
, when the CNC can be renegotiation-proof, the optimal CNC is the one that maximizes the sum of the value of the human capital investment and the value of the labor mobility.
the legal policy of the U.S. states that enforce CNCs is efficient.
the law should enforce CNCs when their scope reasonably protects a legitimate interest of a party.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
, when the parties can commit to a contract, a well-drawn covenant not to compete can be efficient, but when the parties cannot commit, a covenant not to compete will be overbroad and inefficient.
, when the law allows CNCs, it should do so with the understanding that the parties to a contract will tend to overuse them.
the legal enforcement of CNC should be based on the scope of the CNC, not its existence.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the law should be more concerned about the scope of CNCs than their existence.
the legal treatment of CNCs is a policy choice, not an inevitability of economic forces, and that the law can play an active role in the design of efficient contracts.
, when it comes to human capital investment, the law should not be too quick to condemn CNCs, but should be careful to police the contracting parties' incentives to overinvest.
